claim: Docking studies of OGP to both the active and inactive models of CB2 suggest a potential binding site at the extracellular region of CB2.
source: Docking studies of OGP to both the active and inactive models of CB2 were used to predict feasible binding sites of OGP in CB2. These studies did not rule out binding of OGP at the orthosteric domain but suggested another potential binging site - possibly an allosteric site - at the extracellular region of CB2.
evidence: This is a result from computational docking studies.

claim: Docking studies suggest that OGP exhibits higher affinity to the active model of CB2 compared with the inactive model.
source: Furthermore, as one would expect from a receptor agonist, docking calculations suggest that OGP exhibits higher affinity to the active model compared with the inactive model (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from computational docking studies.

claim: Docking calculations suggest that OGP and CP55940 bind to CB2 simultaneously, at distinct sites without reciprocally interfering.
source: These studies also suggested that OGP and CP55940 bind to CB2 simultaneously, at distinct sites without reciprocally interfering.
evidence: This is a result from computational docking studies.

claim: MD simulations with OGP at the proposed binding site within the ECL region show that the peptide stably stays in that region.
source: Indeed, MD simulations with OGP at the proposed binding site within the ECL region show that the peptide stably stays in that region (Figure 3A) with no noticeable changes in the dynamic energy even in the presence of the classical agonist CP55940 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: OGP did not displace tritiated CP55940 in a competition assay.
source: Following up on our docking simulation that supported the notion of a stable binding of OGP in the presence of a lipophilic agonist in the classical intramembranous binding site, we performed here a competition assay between tritiated CP55940 a synthetic lipophilic CB2 agonist, and OGP. Our results showed that OGP did not displace CP55940, suggesting that there is no competition between these agonists at the same binding site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no competition between OGP and CP55940 at the same binding site at CB2.
source: Following up on our docking simulation that supported the notion of a stable binding of OGP in the presence of a lipophilic agonist in the classical intramembranous binding site, we performed here a competition assay between tritiated CP55940 a synthetic lipophilic CB2 agonist, and OGP. Our results showed that OGP did not displace CP55940, suggesting that there is no competition between these agonists at the same binding site (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the competition assay data.

claim: Increasing concentrations of OGP up to 10–10 M resulted in significantly higher CB2 activation by CP55940 as indicated by the stimulation of [35S]GTPγS induced by 0.1 nM CP55940.
source: To this end, we treated hCB2-CHO-derived membranes with CP55940 and measured receptor activation using the GTPγS binding assay (Figure 3D and E). Notably, increasing concentrations of OGP up to 10–10 M resulted in significantly higher CB2 activation by CP55940 as indicated by the stimulation of [35S]GTPγS induced by 0.1 nM CP55940 (Figure 3D) and 10 nM CP55940 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Increasing concentrations of OGP up to 10–10 M resulted in significantly higher CB2 activation by CP55940 as indicated by the stimulation of [35S]GTPγS induced by 10 nM CP55940.
source: To this end, we treated hCB2-CHO-derived membranes with CP55940 and measured receptor activation using the GTPγS binding assay (Figure 3D and E). Notably, increasing concentrations of OGP up to 10–10 M resulted in significantly higher CB2 activation by CP55940 as indicated by the stimulation of [35S]GTPγS induced by 0.1 nM CP55940 (Figure 3D) and 10 nM CP55940 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: OGP binds at an allosteric site at CB2.
source: These results further support the notion that OGP binds at an allosteric site at CB2 and indicate that OGP acts as a PAM in the presence of lipophilic CB2 agonists.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing no competition and positive allosteric modulation.

claim: OGP acts as a PAM in the presence of lipophilic CB2 agonists.
source: These results further support the notion that OGP binds at an allosteric site at CB2 and indicate that OGP acts as a PAM in the presence of lipophilic CB2 agonists.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing positive allosteric modulation.

claim: The effect of OGP on osteoblast proliferation exhibits a biphasic relationship, characterized by a dose-response stimulation at low peptide concentrations, followed by reversal of this enhancement at higher doses.
source: It has been repeatedly demonstrated that the effect of OGP on osteoblast proliferation exhibits a biphasic relationship, characterized by a dose-response stimulation at low peptide concentrations, followed by reversal of this enhancement at higher doses (Miguel et al., 2005; Bab and Chorev, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A similar biphasic effect was reported for cannabinoid ligands.
source: A similar biphasic effect was also reported for cannabinoid ligands (Ofek et al., 2006; Ofek et al., 2011; Smoum et al., 2015) and for other ligands of other GPCRs (Schattauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The osteoblastic proliferative activity of both OGP and HU-910 is characterized by nearly an identical dose response relationship.
source: Indeed, we show here in mouse-derived cultures that the osteoblastic proliferative activity of both OGP and HU-910, a potent CB2-selective agonist (Horváth et al., 2012), is characterized by nearly an identical dose response relationship (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The activity of OGP is completely abrogated following genetic ablation of CB2 in osteoblasts.
source: More importantly, the activity of OGP is completely abrogated following genetic ablation of CB2, as demonstrated using cell count and the bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) assay (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proliferative effect of OGP in murine osteoblasts was abrogated following pharmacological blockade with the CB2-selective antagonist SR144528.
source: The proliferative effect of OGP in both murine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and human osteoblasts (Figure 4C and D) was also abrogated following pharmacological blockade with the CB2-selective antagonist SR144528.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proliferative effect of OGP in human osteoblasts was abrogated following pharmacological blockade with the CB2-selective antagonist SR144528.
source: The proliferative effect of OGP in both murine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and human osteoblasts (Figure 4C and D) was also abrogated following pharmacological blockade with the CB2-selective antagonist SR144528.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The presence of CB2 is essential for OGP activity in osteoblasts.
source: These results indicate that the presence of CB2 is essential for OGP activity in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing loss of OGP activity when CB2 is absent or blocked.

claim: CB2 agonists inhibit osteoclast differentiation in ex vivo cultures of bone marrow monocytes in the presence of M-CSF and RANKL.
source: CB2 agonists inhibit osteoclast differentiation in ex vivo cultures of bone marrow monocytes in the presence of M-CSF and RANKL (Ofek et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OGP has anti-osteoclastogenic activity in cultures derived from WT animals.
source: We show here that OGP shares the same anti-osteoclastogenic activity in cultures derived from WT animals (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The anti-osteoclastogenic effect of OGP is entirely absent in Cnr2-/---derived cultures.
source: By contrast, this effect of OGP is entirely absent in Cnr2-/---derived cultures (Figure 4E and F), demonstrating that the expression of CB2 is essential for mediating the anti-osteoclastogenic effect of OGP.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The expression of CB2 is essential for mediating the anti-osteoclastogenic effect of OGP.
source: By contrast, this effect of OGP is entirely absent in Cnr2-/---derived cultures (Figure 4E and F), demonstrating that the expression of CB2 is essential for mediating the anti-osteoclastogenic effect of OGP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing loss of OGP activity in CB2-deficient cells.

claim: The anabolic effect of OGP and other CB2 agonists in ovariectomized (OVX) mice was reported in separate studies.
source: The anabolic effect of OGP and other CB2 agonists in ovariectomized (OVX) mice was reported in separate studies (Ofek et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2000; Smoum et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Vehicle treated OVX animals (both WT and Cnr2-/-) showed a significant bone loss in the trabecular bone compartment compared with the Sham-OVX control animals.
source: As expected, the vehicle (Veh) treated OVX animals (both WT and Cnr2-/-) showed a significant bone loss in the trabecular bone compartment compared with the Sham-OVX control animals (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There were no significant OVX-induced changes in the cortical bone of the WT mice.
source: There were no significant OVX-induced changes in the cortical bone of the WT mice, but in the Cnr2-/- mice, OVX induced slight but statistically significant decrease in volumetric bone mineral density, diaphyseal diameter, and cortical area over total bone area (–5, –3, and –5%, respectively, vs. Sham, Figure 5K and L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In Cnr2-/- mice, OVX induced slight but statistically significant decrease in volumetric bone mineral density, diaphyseal diameter, and cortical area over total bone area.
source: There were no significant OVX-induced changes in the cortical bone of the WT mice, but in the Cnr2-/- mice, OVX induced slight but statistically significant decrease in volumetric bone mineral density, diaphyseal diameter, and cortical area over total bone area (–5, –3, and –5%, respectively, vs. Sham, Figure 5K and L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5K and L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daily treatment of OVX WT mice with OGP significantly restored BV/TV in the trabecular bone compartment (+45.9% vs. OVX, Veh-treated mice, p=0.035).
source: Daily treatment of OVX mice with OGP significantly restored BV/TV in the trabecular bone compartment (+45.9% vs. OVX, Veh-treated mice, p=0.035, Figure 5A) of WT animals as previously described (Bab and Chorev, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: OGP treatment in OVX WT mice was accompanied with significant increases in trabecular connectivity density and trabecular number (Tb.N) but not trabecular thickness (Tb.Th).
source: This was accompanied with significant increases in trabecular connectivity density and trabecular number (Tb.N) but not trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) (Figure 5B, C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B, C and D.

claim: OGP did not affect any of the cortical bone parameters in the WT OVX mice.
source: OGP did not affect any of the cortical bone parameters in the WT mice (Figure 5E–F and K–L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 A-D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E–F and K–L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 A-D.

claim: OGP had no effect on any of the trabecular and cortical bone parameters in OVX Cnr2-/- animals.
source: Importantly, OGP had no effect on any of the trabecular and cortical bone parameters in OVX Cnr2-/- animals (Figure 5G–L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G–L.

claim: The bone protective capacity of OGP is mediated by CB2.
source: This observation demonstrates that the bone protective capacity of OGP is mediated by CB2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing loss of OGP activity in CB2-deficient mice.

claim: Anti-inflammatory activity is a hallmark of CB2 agonists.
source: Anti-inflammatory activity is a hallmark of CB2 agonists (Sun et al., 2017; Ossola et al., 2016; Malfitano et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LPS induces a dramatic inflammatory response in bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: Gene expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Il1b and Tnfa) indicated that LPS induces a dramatic inflammatory response, and that OGP completely abrogates the expression of these cytokines at 10–14 to 10–12 M doses (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: OGP completely abrogates the expression of Il1b and Tnfa in WT macrophages at 10–14 to 10–12 M doses.
source: Gene expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Il1b and Tnfa) indicated that LPS induces a dramatic inflammatory response, and that OGP completely abrogates the expression of these cytokines at 10–14 to 10–12 M doses (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The effect of OGP on LPS-induced cytokine expression was absent in Cnr2-/- macrophages.
source: Notably, the effect of OGP was absent in Cnr2-/- cells (Figure 6C and D), indicating that the anti-inflammatory effect of the peptide is mediated by CB2.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The anti-inflammatory effect of OGP is mediated by CB2.
source: Notably, the effect of OGP was absent in Cnr2-/- cells (Figure 6C and D), indicating that the anti-inflammatory effect of the peptide is mediated by CB2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing loss of OGP activity in CB2-deficient cells.

claim: CB2 agonists inhibit mast cell degranulation.
source: Consistent with the established inhibition of mast cell degranulation by CB2 agonists (Jonsson et al., 2006), OGP significantly inhibited the effect of xylene on ear swelling (–70%), similar to the CB2-selective agonist HU910 (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OGP significantly inhibited the effect of xylene on ear swelling (–70%) in WT mice.
source: Consistent with the established inhibition of mast cell degranulation by CB2 agonists (Jonsson et al., 2006), OGP significantly inhibited the effect of xylene on ear swelling (–70%), similar to the CB2-selective agonist HU910 (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: HU910 significantly inhibited the effect of xylene on ear swelling in WT mice.
source: Consistent with the established inhibition of mast cell degranulation by CB2 agonists (Jonsson et al., 2006), OGP significantly inhibited the effect of xylene on ear swelling (–70%), similar to the CB2-selective agonist HU910 (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: In Cnr2-/- mice, OGP and HU910 had no effect on ear swelling.
source: However, in Cnr2-/- mice, OGP and HU910 had no effect on ear swelling (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Indomethacin had the same inhibitory effect on ear swelling in WT and Cnr2-/- mice.
source: Because indomethacin had the same inhibitory effect in WT and Cnr2-/- mice, these findings indicate that the effect of OGP is entirely CB2 dependent and distinct from that of prostaglandins.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of OGP on ear swelling is entirely CB2 dependent and distinct from that of prostaglandins.
source: Because indomethacin had the same inhibitory effect in WT and Cnr2-/- mice, these findings indicate that the effect of OGP is entirely CB2 dependent and distinct from that of prostaglandins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing OGP and indomethacin effects.

claim: The ratio between free OGP and total irOGP(1-14) in the serum decreased between the third and the fifth decades of life in men.
source: In a previous study, we reported that the ratio between free OGP and total irOGP(1-14) in the serum decreased between the third and the fifth decades of life in men (Greenberg et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The age range between the third and fifth decades of life is characterized by age-related bone loss in humans, independently of sex hormones.
source: Importantly, this age range is characterized by age-related bone loss in humans, independently of sex hormones (Demontiero et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: During the fifth decade of life, irOGP(1-14) serum levels in premenopausal women are significantly lower than during the third and fourth decades (p=0.039 and p=0.016, respectively).
source: Our analysis revealed that during the fifth decade of life irOGP(1-14) serum levels are significantly lower than during the third and fourth decades (p=0.039 and p=0.016, respectively, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Serum OGP(1-14) and OGP levels decline with age, thus contributing to the reduced CB2 tone and related bone loss.
source: This finding supports the notion that serum OGP(1-14) and OGP levels decline with age, thus contributing to the reduced CB2 tone and related bone loss.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing age-related decline in OGP levels.

claim: Vehicle-treated 6-month-old mice displayed a significant trabecular bone loss (30% reduced BV/TV, 54% reduced Conn.D, and 36% reduced Tb.N; no difference in Tb.Th) relative to the 3-month-old mice (p=0.01).
source: Indeed, Veh-treated mice (6 mo-Veh) displayed a significant trabecular bone loss (30% reduced BV/TV, 54% reduced Conn.D, and 36% reduced Tb.N; no difference in Tb.Th) relative to the 3-month-old mice (p=0.01, Figure 8B–E and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–E and H.

claim: The cortical bone did not show significant changes between the age of 3 and 6 months in vehicle-treated mice.
source: The cortical bone did not show significant changes between the age of 3 and 6 months (Figure 8F–G, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8F–G, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daily administration of 1 µg/kg/day OGP for 3 months completely prevented the trabecular bone loss in mice.
source: Daily administration of 1 µg/kg/day OGP for 3 months completely prevented the trabecular bone loss (Figure 8B–E and H) and had a significant effect on the cortical bone (cortical expansion, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–E and H.

claim: Daily administration of 1 µg/kg/day OGP for 3 months had a significant effect on the cortical bone (cortical expansion).
source: Daily administration of 1 µg/kg/day OGP for 3 months completely prevented the trabecular bone loss (Figure 8B–E and H) and had a significant effect on the cortical bone (cortical expansion, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The OGP-treated mice at 6 months of age displayed bone structural values similar to their 3-month-old counterparts, thus completely preventing the age-related skeletal changes.
source: Overall, the OGP-treated mice at 6 months of age displayed bone structural values similar to their 3-month-old counterparts, thus completely preventing the age-related skeletal changes (Figure 8B–H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–H.

claim: The actions of OGP on CB2-regulated processes are at least equally important to those of the arachidonic acid-derived ECs: 2-AG and AEA.
source: Insights derived from our studies suggest that the actions of OGP on CB2-regulated processes are at least equally important to those of the arachidonic acid-derived ECs: 2-AG and AEA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: OGP rather than the classical ECs is essential for maintaining the CB2 tone in bone during aging.
source: Moreover, our data suggest that OGP rather than the classical ECs is essential for maintaining the CB2 tone in bone during aging.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing no age-related changes in classical ECs but decline in OGP levels.

claim: CB2 plays a major role in suppressing inflammatory responses and related conditions such as neuropathic pain, ischemia/reperfusion injury, and atherosclerosis.
source: Several studies in the last two decades demonstrated a major role for CB2 in suppressing inflammatory responses and related conditions such as neuropathic pain, ischemia/reperfusion injury, and atherosclerosis, as well as protection against age-related bone loss (Ofek et al., 2006; Racz et al., 2008; Prime et al., 2009; Steffens et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CB2 plays a role in protection against age-related bone loss.
source: Several studies in the last two decades demonstrated a major role for CB2 in suppressing inflammatory responses and related conditions such as neuropathic pain, ischemia/reperfusion injury, and atherosclerosis, as well as protection against age-related bone loss (Ofek et al., 2006; Racz et al., 2008; Prime et al., 2009; Steffens et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activity of CB2 agonists is inconsistent with the continuous tone required for attenuating age-related bone loss.
source: This role has been revealed primarily by using phyto- or synthetic cannabinoids rather than ECs, which are unstable, short-lived neurotransmitter-like compounds. The activity of such agonists is inconsistent with the continuous tone required for attenuating age-related bone loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of classical ECs.

claim: Circulating peptide agonists at appropriate concentrations fulfill the function of maintaining CB2 tone.
source: Rather, we hypothesized that circulating peptide agonists at appropriate concentrations fulfill these functions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: OGP and CB2 receptor cannabinoid ligands trigger the same intracellular signaling pathway.
source: The receptor for this peptide has remained unknown for almost three decades, although we showed in separate studies that OGP and CB2 receptor cannabinoid ligands trigger the same intracellular signaling pathway (Miguel et al., 2005; Ofek et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Virtually all living cells may be able to secrete certain amounts of endogenous AEA or 2-AG.
source: Virtually all living cells may be able to secrete certain amounts of endogenous AEA or 2-AG, and the serum used in in vitro assays may contain small amounts of ECs.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about EC production.

claim: OGP can induce CB2 signaling by itself.
source: Our quick assays performed in CHO cells with no serum (Figure 2B) may suggest that OGP can induce CB2 signaling by itself.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Because of its hydrophilic nature and dramatically different molecular structure, OGP is less likely to compete with lipophilic cannabinoid ligands at the classical transmembranous binding site under normal physiological conditions.
source: Because of its hydrophilic nature and dramatically different molecular structure, OGP is less likely to compete with lipophilic cannabinoid ligands (e.g. AEA and 2-AG) at the classical transmembranous binding site under normal physiological conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemical properties of OGP.

claim: The allosteric binding of OGP at CB2 can modulate the orthosteric binding of lipophilic agonists.
source: This lack of competition would suggest that the allosteric binding of OGP at CB2 can modulate the orthosteric binding of lipophilic agonists.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of competition observed in binding assays.

claim: It is unclear whether OGP increases CP55940 binding at CB2 or merely the CB2 functional response to CP55940.
source: From these results, it is still unclear whether OGP increases CP55940 binding at CB2 or merely the CB2 functional response to CP55940.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: Computational docking and MD studies suggest a possible allosteric site for OGP binding at the CB2 receptor.
source: Computational docking and MD studies suggest a possible allosteric site for OGP binding at the CB2 receptor.
evidence: This is a result from computational studies.

claim: The exact binding mode of OGP at CB2 remains uncertain as the exact structure of the N-terminal, which is crucial to the exact binding mode of an allosteric site, is hard to predict.
source: The exact binding mode remains uncertain as the exact structure of the N-terminal, which is crucial to the exact binding mode of an allosteric site, is hard to predict.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging limitations of the computational predictions.

claim: The peptide OGP is very flexible and its conformation is rather elusive.
source: Notably, the peptide is very flexible and its conformation is therefore rather elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural properties of OGP.

claim: OGP can bind to the ECL region of CB2, although the exact binding mode may be slightly different than that obtained from calculations.
source: Hence, our results suggest that OGP can bind to the ECL region, although the exact binding mode may be slightly different than that obtained from our calculations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational studies with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: Pandey et al. suggested a possible allosteric site for dihydro-gambogic acid and trans-β-caryophyllene within the CB2 receptor.
source: Our findings are supported by recent studies of Pandey et al. who also suggested a possible allosteric site for dihydro-gambogic acid and trans-β-caryophyllene within the CB2 receptor (Pandey et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: More comprehensive studies are needed to determine whether OGP is a full agonist at CB2 or a PAM in conjunction with bound orthosteric agonists.
source: More comprehensive studies are needed to determine whether OGP is a full agonist at CB2 or a PAM in conjunction with bound orthosteric agonists.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the need for future research.

claim: CB1 and CB2 share a 30% identity (43% similarity) over the full sequence.
source: Following the recently reported crystal structure of CB2 (47), we estimate that these two receptors share a 30% identity (43% similarity) over the full sequence, 44% identity (62% similarity) without the N- and C-terminal regions, and 51% identity (69% similarity) if only the transmembrane regions are considered (Supplementary file 3; Munk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from sequence analysis based on the crystal structure.

claim: CB1 and CB2 share 44% identity (62% similarity) without the N- and C-terminal regions.
source: Following the recently reported crystal structure of CB2 (47), we estimate that these two receptors share a 30% identity (43% similarity) over the full sequence, 44% identity (62% similarity) without the N- and C-terminal regions, and 51% identity (69% similarity) if only the transmembrane regions are considered (Supplementary file 3; Munk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from sequence analysis based on the crystal structure.

claim: CB1 and CB2 share 51% identity (69% similarity) if only the transmembrane regions are considered.
source: Following the recently reported crystal structure of CB2 (47), we estimate that these two receptors share a 30% identity (43% similarity) over the full sequence, 44% identity (62% similarity) without the N- and C-terminal regions, and 51% identity (69% similarity) if only the transmembrane regions are considered (Supplementary file 3; Munk et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a result from sequence analysis based on the crystal structure.

claim: The homology between CB1 and CB2 in the extracellular regions drops to 38% identity (or even 10% if we consider the N-terminal region).
source: Assuming that the allosteric binding at CB2 involves the extracellular regions where the homology between the two receptors drops to 38% identity (or even 10% if we consider the N-terminal region) reduces the likelihood that OGP also binds to CB1.
evidence: This is a result from sequence analysis.

claim: The lower homology in extracellular regions reduces the likelihood that OGP also binds to CB1.
source: Assuming that the allosteric binding at CB2 involves the extracellular regions where the homology between the two receptors drops to 38% identity (or even 10% if we consider the N-terminal region) reduces the likelihood that OGP also binds to CB1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence homology data.

claim: It cannot be ruled out that under certain conditions OGP binds to CB1.
source: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that under certain conditions OGP binds to CB1.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty.

claim: The reversal of the effect at high doses of OGP likely results from desensitization of the receptor.
source: The reversal of the effect at high doses likely results from desensitization of the receptor (Kelly et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A biphasic effect in vivo was reported for another CB2 agonist.
source: Interestingly, such a biphasic effect in vivo was also reported for another CB2 agonist (Smoum et al., 2015), although the most common observation is a plateau after the optimal dose is reached (Bab et al., 1992; Schattauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The most common observation for CB2 agonists in vivo is a plateau after the optimal dose is reached.
source: Interestingly, such a biphasic effect in vivo was also reported for another CB2 agonist (Smoum et al., 2015), although the most common observation is a plateau after the optimal dose is reached (Bab et al., 1992; Schattauer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of a stable and selective CB2 agonist and PAM is of great significance since the known EC ligands (AEA and 2-AG) are prone to fast enzymatic breakdown, bind to both CB1 and CB2 and elicit different effects on each receptor.
source: The presence of such a stable and selective CB2 agonist and PAM is of great significance since the known EC ligands (AEA and 2-AG) are prone to fast enzymatic breakdown, bind to both CB1 and CB2 and elicit different effects on each receptor.
evidence: This is an inference about the significance of the findings based on known properties of classical ECs.

claim: OGP is a third endogenous cannabinoid with long-lasting effects and CB2 selectivity.
source: This study portrays OGP as a third endogenous cannabinoid with long-lasting effects and CB2 selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB2 selectivity of OGP is particularly relevant in the CNS thus avoiding the psychoactive effect associated with CB1 EC agonists.
source: The latter is particularly relevant in the CNS thus avoiding the psychoactive effect associated with CB1 EC agonists.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of CB2 selectivity.

claim: CB2 has been primarily associated with the immune and skeletal systems in mice and men.
source: Because CB2 has been primarily associated with the immune and skeletal systems in mice and men, it suggests that the main roles of OGP (and its potential therapeutic effects) are in these two systems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CB2 expression and function.

claim: The main roles of OGP (and its potential therapeutic effects) are in the immune and skeletal systems.
source: Because CB2 has been primarily associated with the immune and skeletal systems in mice and men, it suggests that the main roles of OGP (and its potential therapeutic effects) are in these two systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on CB2 expression patterns and OGP's activity at CB2.

claim: Loss-of-function approaches to study the physiological significance of OGP are problematic.
source: Ideally, genetic ablation of OGP could be used to assess the physiological role of OGP. However, these loss-of-function approaches to study the physiological significance of OGP are problematic.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological limitations.

claim: Molecular targeting of OGP, such as by gene ablation or RNA interference, would also target histone H4 expression, which is indispensable for life.
